profiles.meeting_scenario: The team is troubleshooting an internal reverse-debugging feature called "position" that should let engineers jump back to the last write before a corrupted value appears in a mixed Java/C payment service. In recent tests on a Java checkout application that calls a native C pricing library through JNI, the debugger correctly reports a last write for a bad total but replaying to that position lands slightly later than expected and sometimes misses the corruption entirely. The meeting is a 30-minute troubleshooting session between the native debugger owner and the Java runtime instrumentation owner to diagnose whether the issue is in write capture, replay control, or cross-language timestamp handling, and to decide what change to make before an internal demo. The expected outcome is a shared plan for the immediate fix and what they will validate in the next rerun.

members.name: Nina Park
members.expertise: Native runtime instrumentation, GCC passes, replay control, low-level memory tracing
members.background: Nina built the C-side implementation of position by extending the compiler toolchain and integrating it with the team's replay debugger; she usually works on native services and thinks in terms of concrete memory events and instruction boundaries.
members.private_state: Nina wants to protect the upcoming demo by proving the replay controller is fundamentally sound and that any miss is due to incomplete capture coverage rather than a flaw in position semantics.
hidden_assumptions: When people say "last write," they mean the final physical store to the relevant memory address before the bad read, regardless of whether it comes from a helper like memcpy or from generated native code inside JNI.
If replay reaches the same instruction count and memory image just before the store, that is close enough to say position worked, even if the UI highlights the next source-level statement.
The problematic checkout corruption is the native buffer overwrite observed in the JNI pricing path, because that is the incident tied to the memory address she inspected.
Saying "instrument the writes" naturally includes compiler-inserted native stores and expanded library calls in the C component, since that is where hidden overwrites usually occur.

members.name: Omar Singh
members.expertise: Bytecode transformation, JVM debugging hooks, object-field tracing, deterministic test harnesses
members.background: Omar built the Java-side bytecode transformer that assigns timestamps to writes and exposes position to the IDE plugin; he mostly debugs application code and thinks in terms of source-level variables and reproducible user-visible behavior.
members.private_state: Omar wants a narrow, stable fix that keeps JVM overhead low and makes the feature look trustworthy to application developers during the demo.
hidden_assumptions: When people say "last write," they usually mean the last source-level assignment to the corrupted variable or field that a developer can act on, not an incidental native store into adjacent memory.
A fix only counts if replay stops at the source location a Java developer recognizes as the write, with the corrupted value still reproducible from the same request scenario.
The problematic checkout corruption is the wrong Order.total field update seen in the Java service logs, because that is the symptom users and developers noticed.
Saying "instrument the writes" refers to application-level field and array writes in transformed bytecode, not every native memory movement beneath JNI.
The replay run everyone refers to is the deterministic single-request harness captured from the failing checkout, since that is the only environment where timestamp ordering is expected to be stable.

That smells like missing capture around a helper-generated store or memcpy expansion, not broken position semantics.
